title: Waraqa's warning
hook: Waraqa says the same angel came to Musa, and that his people would drive him out (Bukhari)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Khadijah's comfort. She didn't explain the angel; she listed the good he did. Your line was: Allah would never disgrace you.

Good news and bad news, from the same old man, in the same breath. Khadijah has brought her husband to her cousin, Waraqa ibn Nawfal, a learned man, old by now and blind. He listens to the whole account of the cave. Then he tells the Prophet two things: a recognition, and a warning the Prophet doesn't expect. Today: Waraqa's warning.
screen: `AN OLD, BLIND COUSIN LISTENS.` → `FIRST, A RECOGNITION.` → `THEN, A WARNING.`

segments.voice: The account is in Sahih al-Bukhari, told by 'Aishah. She says Waraqa had become a Christian before Islam, and that he wrote, and had copied from the Gospel as much as Allah willed. First he says: this is the Namus, the one Allah sent down to Musa. It is understood as the angel Jibril. Then the warning: I wish I were young. I wish I could be alive when your people drive you out. And the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ asks, in the Arabic, a-wa mukhrijiyya hum? Will they really drive me out? You can hear the surprise. This is the man Mecca called al-Amin, the trustworthy, the one the clans chose to settle the stone. Waraqa's answer is plain: no man has ever come with anything like what you've brought without being treated as an enemy. And if your day reaches me, I will help you with all my strength. A hard truth, told kindly, by someone who puts himself beside it: if I'm there, I'm with you. The warning did come true. The Qur'an, years later, speaks of the time when those who disbelieved drove him out, and of Allah's help to him in the cave. But Waraqa didn't see it. The hadith ends: not long after, Waraqa died, and the revelation paused.
screen: `THIS IS THE NAMUS OF MUSA.` · `WILL THEY REALLY DRIVE ME OUT?` · `NO ONE BROUGHT THIS UNOPPOSED.` · `IF I LIVE, I'M WITH YOU.` · then, large: `THEY WILL DRIVE YOU OUT.`

segments.voice: Think of something true you've been told and haven't wanted to hear, about your health, your work, a relationship, a habit, and let your own 'will they really?' be there without pushing it away. Then think of who told you, and whether, like Waraqa, they stood beside you when they said it; if you pray, ask for the strength to take it in.
Waraqa's warning. Khadijah's old cousin recognized the angel who came to Musa, and told the Prophet his own people would drive him out, and promised to stand with him. Today's word.
Your line: they will drive you out. A hard truth, and a friend standing beside it. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims remember Waraqa ibn Nawfal with respect as the learned cousin of Khadijah who recognized the revelation, and his warning is retold when the beginning of the Prophet's ﷺ mission is taught.

notes: Waraqa's description (became a Christian in the Jahiliyyah; wrote Hebrew/Arabic; copied from the Gospel) follows Bukhari 3; the script says only 'he wrote', since narrations differ on Hebrew or Arabic.
Qur'an 9:40 paraphrased (not quoted) because the exact Pickthall wording was not certain.
'This is the man Mecca called al-Amin' links back to days 715 and 721; confirm acceptable.
The hadith's last line (Waraqa died, the revelation paused) mentioned only as a pointer to tomorrow's 'The pause'; the fatrah itself is not taught here.
Original: confirm the vowel marks of أَوَمُخْرِجِيَّ هُمْ.
Waraqa is described neutrally as a Christian who knew the earlier scriptures; no comparison is drawn between traditions.
